transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello doctor. Thank you for taking the time to see me. You know, I was just telling my neighbor the other day—she’s a lovely woman, always checking in on me since I've gotten older and spend most of my days around the house—I was telling her that I just don't know what gets into me lately. I spend a lot of time in my kitchen, you see. It's a small kitchen, but it's where I make all my old recipes, the ones my mother taught me back before I had to leave high school to help out at home. 

Lately... well, I'll make a big pot of something warm, you know, comfort food. Maybe some heavy stew or macaroni, the kind of food that just makes you feel safe and settled. And I sit down at my little table to have a bowl, just a regular bowl, because at my age, seventy-eight, you really don't need to be eating like a farmhand anymore. But then... it's the strangest thing, doctor. What brings me in is that once I start eating those comfort foods, I finish my bowl and I tell myself, "Maria, that is enough. You are done now." I say it right out loud sometimes! But my hand... my hand still goes back to the pot on the stove. It's like I can’t make myself stop. I just stand there with the spoon, going back for another bite, and another, even though I know I shouldn't be doing it. I just can't seem to stop my own hand, and it's been bothering me so much that I finally thought I ought to come in and ask somebody about it.
Can you tell me more about these times when you can't seem to stop eating — do you feel like you're eating much more rapidly than normal, or until you feel uncomfortably full?

Well, it’s funny you ask about how fast I eat, doctor, because my whole life... my whole life I have always been such a slow eater. My late husband, God rest his soul, he used to tease me terribly about it. He’d say that by the time I finished my supper, it was already time to start cooking breakfast! I always believed in taking my time, you know, chewing every bite and really savoring the recipes my mother passed down to me. There's a certain respect you should have for a good meal, I always thought. 

But lately... when this strange thing happens with the pot on the stove, it’s completely different. I don't even go back to my little table to sit down like a civilized person. I just stand there right by the kitchen counter, leaning against it, and I eat so fast. It's like I'm in some kind of a race, but there's nobody else even in the house to take it away from me! I'm just standing there eating at this terrible speed, and I'm hardly even tasting the food at all. It's just... before one bite is even chewed up, the next bite is already going into my mouth. I don't know why I'm rushing so much. I just stand there staring at the tile backsplash—my husband put those yellow tiles in for me back in the eighties, such a messy job that was—and my hand is just moving so fast, bringing the spoon up over and over before I can even taste what I'm eating. It's so unlike me, it really is, and it just makes me feel so out of sorts because I've never been one to rush my food like a hungry dog.
After these times when you're eating so quickly and can't seem to stop, do you feel upset with yourself or guilty about how much you've eaten?

Oh, doctor... yes. Yes, I do. It’s just... well, it’s a terrible feeling, to be perfectly honest with you. A terrible, heavy feeling right here in my chest. You see, cooking and food, they were always such beautiful things in my family. When I had to leave school in the tenth grade—which broke my mother’s heart, but we just didn't have the money and she needed help with the younger ones—she taught me that feeding people is how you show them you love them. Every time I made her recipes, I felt like I was keeping her memory alive, keeping my husband's memory alive, too. Food meant family. It meant caring for people. 

But after I stand there at the counter and eat like that, so fast and so much... I look down at the empty pot, and I just feel this awful wave of shame wash right over me. I feel so sad, doctor, I could just cry right then and there. I take this beautiful thing that used to mean love and comfort, and I turn it into this... this ugly secret. I feel so guilty that I can't even look at myself in the mirror above the sink. I just quickly wash the pot and put it away so nobody will know. I mean, I go to church every Sunday at St. Jude's—I've sat in the fourth pew on the left for forty years—and I talk to the ladies after mass, and all I can think is, "If they knew what I did in my kitchen, if they knew how I ate like a wild animal, they would be so disgusted with me." I have to hide it from everyone, and it just breaks my heart that I’ve let it come to this. I've turned something so good into something I'm so deeply ashamed of.

When you find yourself going back to the pot and eating even after you've told yourself to stop, do you feel like you're not in control of yourself, or like you can't resist the urge to keep eating no matter how hard you try?

Well, yes, doctor, that's exactly it. That's exactly what I meant when I first sat down here with you today. It's like... it's like I'm completely disconnected from my own body. I remember telling you earlier, I sit there, and I say right out loud, "Maria, that is enough. You are done now." I mean it when I say it, too! I truly do. But then... it's the most frightening feeling, because my brain is saying one thing, but my hand... my hand just picks up that spoon and goes right back to the pot. 

It reminds me of when my sister Rosa—she was the youngest, always getting into trouble—when she was little, she would reach for the cooling cookies on the counter, and my mother would smack her hand with a wooden spoon. Rosa knew she shouldn't, but she just couldn't resist. Only I'm not a little girl reaching for a cookie, I'm a seventy-eight-year-old woman, and there's nobody here to smack my hand! I'm the one telling myself to stop, and I just... I can't. It's like a compulsion, or a motor running that I can't find the switch to turn off. I try so hard, doctor, I grip the edge of the counter sometimes, trying to hold myself back, but the urge is just so strong. It pulls me right back in, and before I know it, I'm eating again, completely out of my own control. It's like I'm a passenger in my own kitchen, just watching myself do something I desperately want to stop doing.
Can you describe exactly what goes through your mind during those moments when your hand goes back to the pot—do you feel like you're completely unable to stop yourself, no matter how hard you try?

Yes, doctor, exactly like I was just telling you. It's exactly that. You ask what goes through my mind, and... well, it's just such a jumble, to be honest. I'm standing there, looking down at the stove—let's say it's my mother's Sunday gravy, the one with the pork ribs that takes all afternoon to simmer, or maybe a big pot of macaroni and cheese. I start eating it because it's just so comforting, you know? The house gets so terribly quiet in the evenings since my husband passed, and those comfort foods... they just wrap around you like a warm blanket. 

But then I realize what I'm doing, and I tell myself, clear as a bell, 'Maria, that is enough.' I say it right out loud! But it's like my brain just completely disconnects from my arm. My hand still goes back to the pot, over and over, like I simply can’t make myself stop. I'm standing there thinking, 'Put the spoon down, Maria, go into the living room, turn on your television programs, call Mrs. Higgins next door, do something else,' but the thoughts just float away like smoke. I just watch my hand dip back into the food, and I feel completely helpless to it. 

You'd think by seventy-eight years old, a woman would have some self-discipline, wouldn't you? My husband always said I was the most stubborn, strong-willed woman he ever met. If I made up my mind about something, that was the end of the discussion. But in those moments at the counter, all that willpower is just gone. I know I'm doing it, I know I want to stop, but the hand just keeps moving. I just can't make it stop.
During these episodes when you're eating rapidly and feel out of control, do you keep eating until you feel uncomfortably full?

Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I do. It’s... well, it’s just awful, doctor. I keep eating and eating, like I was telling you, and I don't stop until... well, until I just can't take another bite without feeling sick. By the time I finally put the spoon down and wash the pot, my stomach feels so tight, so terribly heavy and stretched out. It's not a pleasant fullness, not like after a nice Thanksgiving dinner where you just feel satisfied and maybe a little sleepy. No, this is... this is a painful kind of full. 

I usually have to go right into the living room—the one with the floral wallpaper my husband put up back in '92—and I just collapse into his old brown leather recliner. I have to unbutton my slacks, loosen my waistband completely, just to get a little relief, because I've gone so far past what felt comfortable. I just sit there, feeling so stuffed and heavy, and so angry with myself for letting it happen again. I mean, my mother used to say, 'Maria, your eyes are bigger than your stomach,' when I was a little girl and asked for a second helping of her lasagna. But this isn't my eyes being bigger than my stomach. This is me completely ignoring my stomach until it's practically screaming at me that it can't hold another drop. I just push past the point of being full, right into feeling completely uncomfortable and sick to my stomach. It's just a miserable, miserable feeling, doctor.
Do you usually eat alone during these times when you feel out of control with your eating, or do you try to hide this behavior from others?

Well, I... I live alone now, you see. Ever since my Arthur passed away—it was five years ago this past November, the Tuesday right before Thanksgiving, actually—the house is just empty. So, yes, I'm always alone when this happens. Just me and the hum of the refrigerator. 

But I'll tell you this... if anyone were here, if my daughter Susan came over—she lives two towns away in Westbury, has three lovely children of her own, so busy, you know—but if she were to drop by unannounced while I was standing at the stove eating like that... oh, I would just die of embarrassment. I would absolutely hide it. I wouldn't let her see me. I'd probably drop the spoon right into the sink and pretend I was just stirring the pot or putting away leftovers. 

I remember once, Mrs. Higgins from next door—she's a lovely woman, a bit nosy, always peeking through her blinds—she knocked on the back door to bring over some of her zucchini bread while I was right in the middle of... well, right in the middle of eating a whole box of those little powdered donuts over the sink. I panicked, doctor. I shoved the box into the cabinet under the sink with the cleaning supplies, wiped my mouth on my sleeve like a child, and took three deep breaths before I unlocked the door. My heart was pounding out of my chest! I just couldn't bear the thought of her seeing me like that, out of control, stuffing my face. It's so shameful. A woman my age should have more dignity, shouldn't she? So, yes, I'm alone, but if I wasn't... I'd do everything in my power to make sure nobody ever saw me doing it.

After these episodes of eating rapidly and feeling uncomfortably full, do you ever make yourself sick, use laxatives, or exercise excessively to try to control your weight or get rid of the food you ate?

Oh, heavens no. No, no, I would never do anything like that. I mean, the very thought of making myself sick... it just goes against everything I was taught. My mother, rest her soul, she grew up during the Depression, you know, over in Brooklyn. She used to tell us stories about how they didn't even have enough potatoes to make a proper stew sometimes. So the idea of wasting food, of bringing it back up on purpose... she would have tanned my hide, even at my age! She always said food was a blessing from the Lord, and you don't throw away a blessing. 

And as for laxatives, well, I only take my little fiber supplement that Dr. Evans—my regular doctor, the one with the glasses who always wears those nice bow ties—he recommended it for my digestion. But I'd never take anything just to get rid of the food. It just seems so... violent, almost, to your poor body. 

And exercise? Oh, doctor, my knees just aren't what they used to be. I used to love walking down to the shops, Arthur and I would walk all the way to the park on Sundays, but now? With my arthritis acting up the way it does, especially when the weather turns damp like it has been this past week... well, just getting up from that brown recliner I told you about is a chore some days. So no, I don't go running around the block or doing jumping jacks or anything silly like that. I just sit there, feeling full and miserable and terribly guilty, and I just wait for the feeling to pass. It takes hours, sometimes, but I just sit with it. I don't try to undo it, because... well, I did the crime, so to speak, so I just suffer through the punishment. I just wish I could stop doing the crime in the first place, you know?
Do you find yourself eating large amounts of food even when you’re not actually hungry?

Well, doctor, I... I really couldn't say for sure. I mean, what is hunger, really, at my age? Sometimes I think I'm hungry, but maybe I'm just bored, or lonely, or... well, I just don't know. 

When Arthur was alive, we had a schedule, you see. Breakfast at seven-thirty, a light lunch at noon—usually just half a sandwich and some soup, maybe tomato or chicken noodle, whatever was on sale at the Piggly Wiggly—and then dinner right at six o'clock. We never deviated. You knew when it was time to eat because the clock told you it was time to eat. 

But now? Now the days just sort of bleed together. I might wake up at six, or I might stay in bed until nine if my hip is bothering me. And then I wander into the kitchen, and I see a box of crackers, and I think, 'Well, maybe I'll just have one.' And before I know it, half the box is gone. Was I hungry for those crackers? I don't think my stomach was growling, not like when you've been working out in the yard all afternoon and you come in famished. But my mouth wanted them, or my hands just needed something to do, or... I just don't know how to explain it. 

It's like the food is just there, calling to me, and I eat it whether my stomach is asking for it or not. I'll just stand there at the counter—the one with the yellow formica that Arthur swore he was going to replace but never got around to—and I'll just keep putting things in my mouth. A piece of cheese, a handful of pretzels, maybe a leftover dinner roll from the bakery down the street... and I'm not thinking about whether I'm hungry. I'm just eating. So, I suppose I must be eating when I'm not hungry, because I can't remember the last time I actually felt a real, honest-to-goodness hunger pang before one of these... these episodes. It's more of a compulsion, like a restless feeling in my chest, rather than a rumble in my tummy. Does that make any sense, doctor? Because it barely makes sense to me, to be perfectly honest with you.
Can you tell me if these episodes of eating out of control happen more often when you're feeling sad, anxious, or stressed?

Oh, well... sad, anxious, stressed... I don't really know if I can say yes or no to that, doctor. I just haven't really noticed a clear pattern like that, to be perfectly honest with you. 

I mean, I suppose I'm sad a lot of the time, naturally. Losing Arthur... well, you don't just get over something like that, do you? We were married for fifty-two years. Fifty-two years! We met at a dance hall back in the day, he was wearing this sharp blue suit that his mother had bought him for his birthday, and... well, anyway, I miss him every single day. The house is just so dreadfully quiet without him puttering around in the garage or asking me where he left his reading glasses. So, am I sad when I eat? I suppose I'm a little bit sad all the time nowadays, just a sort of low ache in the background, you know? But it's hard to say if the sadness is what actually *makes* me do it. It doesn't seem like I'm sitting there crying my eyes out and then suddenly reaching for a box of cookies, if that makes sense. 

And stressed? Well, heavens, what do I have to be stressed about at my age? I don't have a boss yelling at me, I don't have to worry about getting the kids to school on time like my Susan does. Oh, Susan is always stressed, running here and there, soccer practice, piano lessons, making sure her husband's shirts are pressed... but me? I just sit in my chair. I watch the evening news sometimes, and goodness, I suppose that can make a person anxious, all the terrible things happening in the world today. And the prices at the grocery store! Did you know a carton of eggs is nearly five dollars now at the Piggly Wiggly? It's absolute highway robbery, especially when you're living on a fixed income like I am. But I don't think watching the news or worrying about the price of eggs makes me run into the kitchen and lose control. 

So, no, I haven't really noticed that it happens more when I'm feeling a certain way. It just sort of... happens. Sometimes I'm just sitting there having a perfectly nice, quiet morning, listening to the radio—I like that station that plays the oldies, the real oldies, not this loud noise they call music today—and the next thing I know, I'm standing in the pantry. It doesn't feel like I'm trying to eat away a bad mood or calm my nerves or anything like that. It just creeps up on me out of nowhere, whether it's a good day or a bad day. I just really don't know why it starts.
During these episodes when you feel out of control with your eating, would you say you're eating much more rapidly than normal?

Oh, my, yes. And that's really one of the strangest parts of all this, doctor. Because, you see, I have always, always been such a slow eater. Just famously slow! My mother used to scold me when I was a little girl, sitting there at the kitchen table long after my brothers had run off outside to play, just chewing and chewing my green beans. And Arthur used to tease me about it, too. We'd go out for our anniversary to the nice steakhouse downtown—the one with the red leather booths, you know the one?—and he'd be completely finished with his prime rib while I was still delicately cutting up my baked potato. I always believed in savoring your food, taking your time. 

But lately... well, when this happens, it's like I'm a completely different person. I don't sit down at the table with a proper place setting at all. I just stand there right by the counter—that same yellow formica counter I was telling you about earlier—and I just eat so incredibly fast. It's almost frantic. I'm just putting the food in, one piece right after another, and I'm hardly even tasting it. 

It's like... well, before I've even finished chewing the first bite, the next bite is already in my mouth! It's just shovel it in, swallow, shovel it in. It's so terribly unladylike. If anyone ever walked in and saw me doing it, standing there eating at that speed like I'm afraid someone's going to snatch it away from me, I think I would just die of embarrassment. But there's no one here to snatch it, it's just me and the quiet house. I don't know why I rush so much, but I just fly right through it without even enjoying a single bit of the flavor.
During these times when you're eating rapidly and can't seem to stop, would you say you feel a complete loss of control, like you're unable to stop eating even though you want to?

Oh, doctor, that is exactly it. It's the most dreadful, helpless feeling in the world. Because I do want to stop! I really, truly do. 

I'll be standing there in the kitchen, maybe I've made a little pot of something warm, you know, one of those comfort foods. Sometimes I make a small batch of my mother's macaroni and cheese—the baked kind, with the breadcrumbs on top, not that powdered nonsense in the cardboard box that Susan feeds her kids when she's rushing them off to their piano lessons. I always use a nice sharp cheddar, though it's getting so expensive I have to wait for a coupon. 

Well, anyway, I'll start eating it, just standing right there by the stove, and in my own head, I am having a full conversation with myself. I'll literally say to myself, "Maria, that is enough." I'll tell myself to just put the wooden spoon down, to get some Tupperware out of the bottom drawer and put the rest away in the Frigidaire for tomorrow's lunch. I know I should stop. I want to stop. 

But... well, it's like there's a complete disconnect between my brain and my body. Even while I'm telling myself that I'm done, my hand just goes right back to the pot. It just keeps scooping and going to my mouth, like I absolutely cannot make myself stop, no matter how much I scold myself. It's like I'm a passenger in my own kitchen, just watching my hand go back to the pot again and again. It's really what finally made me realize I needed to come in and talk to someone, because I've never been the sort of person who couldn't control her own hands, you know? It's just so frightening to tell yourself "no" and then watch yourself do it anyway.

target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks if the patient feels a lack of control or an inability to resist the urge to keep eating, which corresponds to the Loss of Control symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, doctor, that's exactly it. That's exactly what I meant when I first sat down here with you today. It's like... it's like I'm completely disconnected from my own body. I remember telling you earlier, I sit there, and I say right out loud, "Maria, that is enough. You are done now." I mean it when I say it, too! I truly do. But then... it's the most frightening feeling, because my brain is saying one thing, but my hand... my hand just picks up that spoon and goes right back to the pot. 

It reminds me of when my sister Rosa—she was the youngest, always getting into trouble—when she was little, she would reach for the cooling cookies on the counter, and my mother would smack her hand with a wooden spoon. Rosa knew she shouldn't, but she just couldn't resist. Only I'm not a little girl reaching for a cookie, I'm a seventy-eight-year-old woman, and there's nobody here to smack my hand! I'm the one telling myself to stop, and I just... I can't. It's like a compulsion, or a motor running that I can't find the switch to turn off. I try so hard, doctor, I grip the edge of the counter sometimes, trying to hold myself back, but the urge is just so strong. It pulls me right back in, and before I know it, I'm eating again, completely out of my own control. It's like I'm a passenger in my own kitchen, just watching myself do something I desperately want to stop doing.

inference.note: The patient's description of feeling a lack of control over eating, eating much more rapidly than normal, and experiencing significant distress and guilt afterward supports narrowing the candidates. The presentation is consistent with loss of control eating, pointing more strongly toward F50.2 (Binge eating disorder) and F50.9 (Eating disorder, unspecified). F94.9 (Selective mutism) has been ruled out as it is unrelated to the reported symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a loss of control over eating during these episodes, which is a key distinguishing feature of Binge Eating Disorder (F50.9) versus Eating Disorder Not Otherwise Specified (F50.2).
doctor.question: Can you describe exactly what goes through your mind during those moments when your hand goes back to the pot—do you feel like you're completely unable to stop yourself, no matter how hard you try?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that once I start eating those comfort foods, I tell myself, 'Maria, that is enough,' but my hand still goes back to the pot like I can’t make myself stop.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for more details about the feeling of being unable to stop eating and the sense of lacking control during the episode.

patient.answer:
Yes, doctor, exactly like I was just telling you. It's exactly that. You ask what goes through my mind, and... well, it's just such a jumble, to be honest. I'm standing there, looking down at the stove—let's say it's my mother's Sunday gravy, the one with the pork ribs that takes all afternoon to simmer, or maybe a big pot of macaroni and cheese. I start eating it because it's just so comforting, you know? The house gets so terribly quiet in the evenings since my husband passed, and those comfort foods... they just wrap around you like a warm blanket. 

But then I realize what I'm doing, and I tell myself, clear as a bell, 'Maria, that is enough.' I say it right out loud! But it's like my brain just completely disconnects from my arm. My hand still goes back to the pot, over and over, like I simply can’t make myself stop. I'm standing there thinking, 'Put the spoon down, Maria, go into the living room, turn on your television programs, call Mrs. Higgins next door, do something else,' but the thoughts just float away like smoke. I just watch my hand dip back into the food, and I feel completely helpless to it. 

You'd think by seventy-eight years old, a woman would have some self-discipline, wouldn't you? My husband always said I was the most stubborn, strong-willed woman he ever met. If I made up my mind about something, that was the end of the discussion. But in those moments at the counter, all that willpower is just gone. I know I'm doing it, I know I want to stop, but the hand just keeps moving. I just can't make it stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient eats until uncomfortably full, which is a key distinguishing feature between F50.2 (Binge Eating Disorder) and F50.9 (Eating Disorder, Unspecified).
doctor.question: During these episodes when you're eating rapidly and feel out of control, do you keep eating until you feel uncomfortably full?

target_item.name: Eating_Until_Uncomfortably_Full
target_item.manifestation: By the time I stop, my stomach feels tight and heavy, and I have to sit in my recliner with my waistband loosened because I went past what felt comfortable.
target_item.reason: The doctor is explicitly asking if I keep eating until I feel uncomfortably full, which matches this symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I do. It’s... well, it’s just awful, doctor. I keep eating and eating, like I was telling you, and I don't stop until... well, until I just can't take another bite without feeling sick. By the time I finally put the spoon down and wash the pot, my stomach feels so tight, so terribly heavy and stretched out. It's not a pleasant fullness, not like after a nice Thanksgiving dinner where you just feel satisfied and maybe a little sleepy. No, this is... this is a painful kind of full. 

I usually have to go right into the living room—the one with the floral wallpaper my husband put up back in '92—and I just collapse into his old brown leather recliner. I have to unbutton my slacks, loosen my waistband completely, just to get a little relief, because I've gone so far past what felt comfortable. I just sit there, feeling so stuffed and heavy, and so angry with myself for letting it happen again. I mean, my mother used to say, 'Maria, your eyes are bigger than your stomach,' when I was a little girl and asked for a second helping of her lasagna. But this isn't my eyes being bigger than my stomach. This is me completely ignoring my stomach until it's practically screaming at me that it can't hold another drop. I just push past the point of being full, right into feeling completely uncomfortable and sick to my stomach. It's just a miserable, miserable feeling, doctor.

inference.note: The patient confirms eating until uncomfortably full, which is consistent with the criteria for Binge Eating Disorder (F50.2). However, insufficient information is available to rule out Eating Disorder, Unspecified (F50.9) at this time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient eats alone due to embarrassment, which is a distinguishing feature of Binge Eating Disorder (F50.9) compared to Eating Disorder Not Otherwise Specified (F50.2).
doctor.question: Do you usually eat alone during these times when you feel out of control with your eating, or do you try to hide this behavior from others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient eats alone or hides their eating behavior due to embarrassment, which corresponds to symptom S054 (Eating alone because of feeling embarrassed by how much one is eating). This symptom is not present in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I live alone now, you see. Ever since my Arthur passed away—it was five years ago this past November, the Tuesday right before Thanksgiving, actually—the house is just empty. So, yes, I'm always alone when this happens. Just me and the hum of the refrigerator. 

But I'll tell you this... if anyone were here, if my daughter Susan came over—she lives two towns away in Westbury, has three lovely children of her own, so busy, you know—but if she were to drop by unannounced while I was standing at the stove eating like that... oh, I would just die of embarrassment. I would absolutely hide it. I wouldn't let her see me. I'd probably drop the spoon right into the sink and pretend I was just stirring the pot or putting away leftovers. 

I remember once, Mrs. Higgins from next door—she's a lovely woman, a bit nosy, always peeking through her blinds—she knocked on the back door to bring over some of her zucchini bread while I was right in the middle of... well, right in the middle of eating a whole box of those little powdered donuts over the sink. I panicked, doctor. I shoved the box into the cabinet under the sink with the cleaning supplies, wiped my mouth on my sleeve like a child, and took three deep breaths before I unlocked the door. My heart was pounding out of my chest! I just couldn't bear the thought of her seeing me like that, out of control, stuffing my face. It's so shameful. A woman my age should have more dignity, shouldn't she? So, yes, I'm alone, but if I wasn't... I'd do everything in my power to make sure nobody ever saw me doing it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient engages in compensatory behaviors (e.g., self-induced vomiting, laxative use, excessive exercise) after episodes of overeating, which would support a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa (F50.2) over binge eating disorder (F50.9).
doctor.question: After these episodes of eating rapidly and feeling uncomfortably full, do you ever make yourself sick, use laxatives, or exercise excessively to try to control your weight or get rid of the food you ate?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about compensatory behaviors such as purging, using laxatives, or excessive exercise, which are not part of the patient's symptom profile for Binge-Eating Disorder.

patient.answer:
Oh, heavens no. No, no, I would never do anything like that. I mean, the very thought of making myself sick... it just goes against everything I was taught. My mother, rest her soul, she grew up during the Depression, you know, over in Brooklyn. She used to tell us stories about how they didn't even have enough potatoes to make a proper stew sometimes. So the idea of wasting food, of bringing it back up on purpose... she would have tanned my hide, even at my age! She always said food was a blessing from the Lord, and you don't throw away a blessing. 

And as for laxatives, well, I only take my little fiber supplement that Dr. Evans—my regular doctor, the one with the glasses who always wears those nice bow ties—he recommended it for my digestion. But I'd never take anything just to get rid of the food. It just seems so... violent, almost, to your poor body. 

And exercise? Oh, doctor, my knees just aren't what they used to be. I used to love walking down to the shops, Arthur and I would walk all the way to the park on Sundays, but now? With my arthritis acting up the way it does, especially when the weather turns damp like it has been this past week... well, just getting up from that brown recliner I told you about is a chore some days. So no, I don't go running around the block or doing jumping jacks or anything silly like that. I just sit there, feeling full and miserable and terribly guilty, and I just wait for the feeling to pass. It takes hours, sometimes, but I just sit with it. I don't try to undo it, because... well, I did the crime, so to speak, so I just suffer through the punishment. I just wish I could stop doing the crime in the first place, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient eats large amounts of food when not physically hungry.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself eating large amounts of food even when you’re not actually hungry?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient eats large amounts of food when not physically hungry, which corresponds to a specific binge-eating disorder criterion (often S053) that is not included in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, I... I really couldn't say for sure. I mean, what is hunger, really, at my age? Sometimes I think I'm hungry, but maybe I'm just bored, or lonely, or... well, I just don't know. 

When Arthur was alive, we had a schedule, you see. Breakfast at seven-thirty, a light lunch at noon—usually just half a sandwich and some soup, maybe tomato or chicken noodle, whatever was on sale at the Piggly Wiggly—and then dinner right at six o'clock. We never deviated. You knew when it was time to eat because the clock told you it was time to eat. 

But now? Now the days just sort of bleed together. I might wake up at six, or I might stay in bed until nine if my hip is bothering me. And then I wander into the kitchen, and I see a box of crackers, and I think, 'Well, maybe I'll just have one.' And before I know it, half the box is gone. Was I hungry for those crackers? I don't think my stomach was growling, not like when you've been working out in the yard all afternoon and you come in famished. But my mouth wanted them, or my hands just needed something to do, or... I just don't know how to explain it. 

It's like the food is just there, calling to me, and I eat it whether my stomach is asking for it or not. I'll just stand there at the counter—the one with the yellow formica that Arthur swore he was going to replace but never got around to—and I'll just keep putting things in my mouth. A piece of cheese, a handful of pretzels, maybe a leftover dinner roll from the bakery down the street... and I'm not thinking about whether I'm hungry. I'm just eating. So, I suppose I must be eating when I'm not hungry, because I can't remember the last time I actually felt a real, honest-to-goodness hunger pang before one of these... these episodes. It's more of a compulsion, like a restless feeling in my chest, rather than a rumble in my tummy. Does that make any sense, doctor? Because it barely makes sense to me, to be perfectly honest with you.

inference.note: The patient reports eating large amounts of food even when not physically hungry, which supports the diagnostic criteria for binge eating disorder (F50.2). No new disorders were introduced, and no existing candidates were ruled out.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a loss of control over eating, specifically if the behavior occurs in response to emotional triggers.
doctor.question: Can you tell me if these episodes of eating out of control happen more often when you're feeling sad, anxious, or stressed?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional triggers for the binge eating episodes (feeling sad, anxious, or stressed beforehand), which is not covered by any of the items in the symptom profile. The profile includes negative affect *after* the binge (S055), but not emotional triggers prior to it.

patient.answer:
Oh, well... sad, anxious, stressed... I don't really know if I can say yes or no to that, doctor. I just haven't really noticed a clear pattern like that, to be perfectly honest with you. 

I mean, I suppose I'm sad a lot of the time, naturally. Losing Arthur... well, you don't just get over something like that, do you? We were married for fifty-two years. Fifty-two years! We met at a dance hall back in the day, he was wearing this sharp blue suit that his mother had bought him for his birthday, and... well, anyway, I miss him every single day. The house is just so dreadfully quiet without him puttering around in the garage or asking me where he left his reading glasses. So, am I sad when I eat? I suppose I'm a little bit sad all the time nowadays, just a sort of low ache in the background, you know? But it's hard to say if the sadness is what actually *makes* me do it. It doesn't seem like I'm sitting there crying my eyes out and then suddenly reaching for a box of cookies, if that makes sense. 

And stressed? Well, heavens, what do I have to be stressed about at my age? I don't have a boss yelling at me, I don't have to worry about getting the kids to school on time like my Susan does. Oh, Susan is always stressed, running here and there, soccer practice, piano lessons, making sure her husband's shirts are pressed... but me? I just sit in my chair. I watch the evening news sometimes, and goodness, I suppose that can make a person anxious, all the terrible things happening in the world today. And the prices at the grocery store! Did you know a carton of eggs is nearly five dollars now at the Piggly Wiggly? It's absolute highway robbery, especially when you're living on a fixed income like I am. But I don't think watching the news or worrying about the price of eggs makes me run into the kitchen and lose control. 

So, no, I haven't really noticed that it happens more when I'm feeling a certain way. It just sort of... happens. Sometimes I'm just sitting there having a perfectly nice, quiet morning, listening to the radio—I like that station that plays the oldies, the real oldies, not this loud noise they call music today—and the next thing I know, I'm standing in the pantry. It doesn't feel like I'm trying to eat away a bad mood or calm my nerves or anything like that. It just creeps up on me out of nowhere, whether it's a good day or a bad day. I just really don't know why it starts.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient eats much more rapidly than normal during these episodes, as this is a key distinguishing feature between the two candidate diagnoses.
doctor.question: During these episodes when you feel out of control with your eating, would you say you're eating much more rapidly than normal?

target_item.name: Rapid_Eating
target_item.manifestation: I have always been a slow eater, but lately when this happens I eat fast standing by the counter, hardly tasting the food before the next bite is already in my mouth.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks if I am eating much more rapidly than normal during the episodes.

patient.answer:
Oh, my, yes. And that's really one of the strangest parts of all this, doctor. Because, you see, I have always, always been such a slow eater. Just famously slow! My mother used to scold me when I was a little girl, sitting there at the kitchen table long after my brothers had run off outside to play, just chewing and chewing my green beans. And Arthur used to tease me about it, too. We'd go out for our anniversary to the nice steakhouse downtown—the one with the red leather booths, you know the one?—and he'd be completely finished with his prime rib while I was still delicately cutting up my baked potato. I always believed in savoring your food, taking your time. 

But lately... well, when this happens, it's like I'm a completely different person. I don't sit down at the table with a proper place setting at all. I just stand there right by the counter—that same yellow formica counter I was telling you about earlier—and I just eat so incredibly fast. It's almost frantic. I'm just putting the food in, one piece right after another, and I'm hardly even tasting it. 

It's like... well, before I've even finished chewing the first bite, the next bite is already in my mouth! It's just shovel it in, swallow, shovel it in. It's so terribly unladylike. If anyone ever walked in and saw me doing it, standing there eating at that speed like I'm afraid someone's going to snatch it away from me, I think I would just die of embarrassment. But there's no one here to snatch it, it's just me and the quiet house. I don't know why I rush so much, but I just fly right through it without even enjoying a single bit of the flavor.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a loss of control during eating episodes, which is a key distinguishing factor between the remaining diagnostic candidates.
doctor.question: During these times when you're eating rapidly and can't seem to stop, would you say you feel a complete loss of control, like you're unable to stop eating even though you want to?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that once I start eating those comfort foods, I tell myself, 'Maria, that is enough,' but my hand still goes back to the pot like I can’t make myself stop.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question specifically asks about feeling a complete loss of control and the inability to stop eating, which directly matches the Loss_of_Control symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh, doctor, that is exactly it. It's the most dreadful, helpless feeling in the world. Because I do want to stop! I really, truly do. 

I'll be standing there in the kitchen, maybe I've made a little pot of something warm, you know, one of those comfort foods. Sometimes I make a small batch of my mother's macaroni and cheese—the baked kind, with the breadcrumbs on top, not that powdered nonsense in the cardboard box that Susan feeds her kids when she's rushing them off to their piano lessons. I always use a nice sharp cheddar, though it's getting so expensive I have to wait for a coupon. 

Well, anyway, I'll start eating it, just standing right there by the stove, and in my own head, I am having a full conversation with myself. I'll literally say to myself, "Maria, that is enough." I'll tell myself to just put the wooden spoon down, to get some Tupperware out of the bottom drawer and put the rest away in the Frigidaire for tomorrow's lunch. I know I should stop. I want to stop. 

But... well, it's like there's a complete disconnect between my brain and my body. Even while I'm telling myself that I'm done, my hand just goes right back to the pot. It just keeps scooping and going to my mouth, like I absolutely cannot make myself stop, no matter how much I scold myself. It's like I'm a passenger in my own kitchen, just watching my hand go back to the pot again and again. It's really what finally made me realize I needed to come in and talk to someone, because I've never been the sort of person who couldn't control her own hands, you know? It's just so frightening to tell yourself "no" and then watch yourself do it anyway.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's primary concern or reason for seeking psychiatric evaluation.
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the full DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for Binge Eating Disorder, including recurrent episodes of eating large amounts of food rapidly in a discrete period of time, feeling a lack of control during the episodes, eating until uncomfortably full, eating when not hungry, eating alone due to embarrassment, and experiencing feelings of shame and guilt afterward. There is no evidence of compensatory behaviors (e.g., purging, excessive exercise) and the behavior does not occur exclusively during the course of another eating disorder such as anorexia or bulimia.
